To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) persistence with therapy was greater in patients on ARB and ACE inhibitor monotherapy; 2) the decrease in blood pressure was greater in patients taking ARB, ACE inhibitor, or CCB monotherapy; and 3) patients on diuretic therapy were the least likely to continue their antihypertensives.

(a) persistence with antihypetensive therapy is higher in patients receiving ARBs or ACE inhibitors than in those receiving diuretics; (b) persistence with antineptensive therapy is lower in patients receiving beta-blockers than in those receiving ARBs; and (c) persistence with antieiptensive therapy is lower with diuretics than with ACE inhibitors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the persistence of treatment with different classes of drugs in a population of elderly, uncomplicated hypertensive patients, and the extent of blood pressure control achieved.
the persistence of treatment and blood pressures control of elderly hypertensive patients, who were treated with different classes.
the persistence of treatment and the extent to which blood pressure (BP)-control was achieved in elderly, uncomplicated hypertensive patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the persistence on treatment and control of hypertension were better in the group treated with angiotensine II receptor blockers than in the group treated by the other classes of antihyperensive drugs.
the persistence on treatment was better with ARBs and ACE inhibitors and worse with diuretics and beta-blockers.

ARBs and ACE inhibitors are more effective than other classes of drugs in terms of both persistence on therapy and blood pressure control, whereas the beta-blocker class is less effective than other drugs in this respect.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the persistence with antihypertenstive therapy is higher with angiotensine receptor blockers and angiotensine converting enzyme inhibitors than with diuretics and beta-blockers.
the use of ARBs or ACE inhibitors is associated with a higher rate of persistence on initial antihyperten- sive treatment and a greater BP control in elderly patients with uncomplicated hypertension.
the use of ARBs, ACE inhibitors, and CCBs is more likely to lead to persistence on treatment and better BP control in elderly patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of ACE inhibitors or CCBs as monotherapy is associated with a higher persistence rate on treatment and a better BP control than diuretics or beta-blockers in elderly uncomplicated hypertensive patients.
persistence with antihypetnsive therapy is better in those treated with ACE inhibitors and CCBs than those treated with beta blockers and diuretics.
